chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who died and left a debt upon him, and left a slave; the slave had wealth in trade, and a son, and in the hand of the slave was wealth and merchandise, and upon the slave was a debt which the slave had borrowed during the lifetime of his master in his trade. And the inheritors and the creditors of the deceased disputed regarding what was in the hand of the slave from the wealth and the merchandise, and regarding the neck (ownership) of the slave.

So he (peace be upon him) said: 'I view that there is no way for the inheritors upon the neck of the slave, nor upon what is in his hand from the merchandise and the wealth, except if they assume responsibility for the debt of all the creditors, then the slave and whatever is in his hand from the wealth would be for the inheritors. But if they refuse, the slave and whatever is in his hand would be for the creditors. The slave and whatever is in his hand from the wealth would be evaluated, then that would be distributed among them by shares.'

So if the price of the slave and whatever is in his hand is insufficient for the wealth of the creditors, they return upon the inheritors for what remains for them, if the deceased had left anything. He said: 'And if there is excess from the price of the slave and whatever was in his hand from the debt of the creditors, it is returned to the inheritors.'

key_terms.رَقَبَةِ الْعَبْدِ: Ownership or neck of the slave

ai.seo_question: How are debts incurred by a slave during his master's lifetime handled after the master's death?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) provides a nuanced juristic solution to the complex intersection of inheritance and debt, prioritizing the creditor's claim on the slave's person and assets while protecting the heirs' residual rights. This ruling reflects the Shia legal principle that a slave's earnings and debts incurred during the master's lifetime are intrinsically linked to the master's estate, ensuring equitable distribution among creditors before heirs receive any surplus. The hadith highlights the practical application of 'al-ghurm bi al-ghinm' (liability accompanies profit) in pre-modern commercial contexts.

en.hubeali: Humeyd Bin Ziyad, from Al Hassan Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ibn Raib, from Zurara who said,

‘I asked Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> about a man who died and left debts upon him, and left a slave for whom was some wealth in the business, and a son, and in the hands of the slave was the wealth, and merchandise, and upon him were debts which the slave had incurred during the lifetime of his master in his business, and the inheritors and the creditors of the deceased disputed regarding what was in the hands of the slave, from the wealth and the merchandise, and regarding the neck (ownership) of the slave’.

So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘I<sup>asws</sup> view that there is no way for the inheritors upon the neck of the slave, nor upon what is in his hands from the merchandise and the wealth, except if they assume responsibility of the debts of the creditors altogether, then the slave and whatever in his hands from the wealth would be for the inheritors. But, if they were to refuse, the slave and whatever is in his hand would be for the creditors. The slave would be evaluated along with whatever is in his hands from the wealth, then that would be distributed between then with proportionately.

So, if the price of the slave and whatever is his hands from the wealth is insufficient for the creditors, they can return upon the inheritors with regards to what remains for them, if the deceased had left anything (else)’. And if there was excess from the price of the slave and whatever was in his hands, from the creditors, it would be returned upon the inheritors’.
en.sarwar: 2. Humayd ibn Ziyad has narrated from al-Hassan ibn Muhammad from ibn Mahbub from ibn Ri’ab from Zurarah who has said the following:

“This is concerning my question before abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who dies owing a certain amount of debts and leaves behind a slave who has his assets in business and a son. In the hand of the slave he leaves the assets, goods and debts owed by the slave which he had incurred during the lifetime of his master for business. The heir and creditors dispute about what is in the hand of the slave, the slave himself and the assets and goods.

He (the Imam) said, ‘In my view the heirs have no say about the slave or about what is in his hand of assets and goods, except if they take responsibility for the debt for all the creditors. Thereafter the slave and what is in his hand of the assets and goods all go in the hands of the heirs; but if they refuse to take responsibility, the slave and all that is in his hand go to the creditors. The slave and whatever is in his hand of the assets are distributed among the creditors proportionate to their shares.

If the slave and the asset could not pay the debts the creditors can ask the heirs for the remaining liabilities if the deceased has left anything. If the slave and assets exceed the debts the remaining goes to the heirs.’”
